title: Threshold City
description: On places where the street ends and a conversation begins.
excerpt: In the morning the threshold is still cool. It holds half a step and the whole decision to stop. Across the street someone lifts a blind, and for a moment the city turns out to be not a set of buildings but a run of small openings.

The threshold is in no hurry to belong to the outside or to the room. It takes the rain, a shoe print and a neighbour's quick question. We do not mark such places on a map: we know them by the pace at which we start to walk.

title: Staircase Margins
description: A short read about moving between floors.
excerpt: A stairwell has its own sentence. The first step begins it, the landing adds a comma, and the window lets you breathe in. As you climb, it is not only the height that changes: the sounds of the street slowly turn into a memory.
On the handrail shines a strip polished by palms. No drawing describes this surface exactly. Here architecture does not end at the layer of paint; it carries on in every everyday touch.

title: A Cup's Distance
description: Everyday things as a measure of time and attention.
excerpt: Between the cup and the window there is room for a morning. You cannot measure it in centimetres: one day it is as short as a glance, the next it stretches until the first bus goes by. A ring stays on the table.
A cup is a small agreement with time. While it is warm, there is still no need to hurry anywhere. Things do not speak for us, but sometimes they offer a place to begin a sentence.

title: Second Bench
description: On staying in a public place with no urgent purpose.
excerpt: The first bench is for waiting. The second is simply for sitting. The difference is small until you notice how your shoulders change when you no longer have to look out for someone arriving.

Over a day, a tree's shadow crosses three boards. The people sitting there leave before this slow movement is finished. Sometimes the length of a city is easier to understand by stopping than by walking it.
